newsitem.title: USA: Competition clouds U.S. reinsurers' growth.
newsitem.headline: Competition clouds U.S. reinsurers' growth.

text.p: Reinsurers are likely to post higher second-quarter earnings than a year ago, but competition remains fierce and premium growth is uninspiring, analysts said.

The tough conditions could prompt further consolidation in an already challenged industry, they said. Among the companies seen as possible acquisition targets are NAC Re Corp, Chartwell Re Corp and Trenwick Group Inc.
"It's a tough environment out there, and we could see companies responding accordingly, by consolidating," said Stuart Shaw, co-managing partner of the Branche Research Group in Tucson, Ariz.

Mild weather and an ensuing absence of major claims, coupled with too much competition, are keeping rates soft. Investors should find it somewhat disturbing that reinsurers' growth is generally coming from underwriting results and investment income, rather than premium income, he said.
"If you're not growing your top line, eventually that's going to impact your bottom line," Shaw said.
"This could be a prelude to a tougher earnings environment down the road."
"Underwriting and investment results will be high, but premium growth will be very limited," said Ira Zuckerman, vice president of research at Nutmeg Securities in Vermont.
"The average industry growth will be in the low single digits, for premium or top line ," he said.
Industry giant General Re Corp is expected to post second-quarter earnings growth of 10.2 percent to $2.92 per share, according to the First Call consensus of analysts' estimates.

Bermuda-based reinsurers have been particularly hard-hit by the soft industry conditions, because they have greater exposure to the catastrophe market, which has seen steep price declines, analysts said.
Among the reinsurers based there is PartnerRe Ltd, which is expected to post a slight earnings decline of 1.8 percent to $1.11 per share.
Another cause for concern is the emergence of the capital markets as a new source of capacity for insurers. This means yet more competition for reinsurers, analysts said.
A landmark event occurred in June, when United Services Automobile Association sold $400 million of so-called "disaster bonds," an issue which was very well-received by the market, analysts said.
"The question is, does this mechanism become broader to include other kinds of reinsurance risks?" said Shaw.
"For the investor, we're not too positive on the reinsurance industry."
